output.title: What capacity limits usually hide
output.body:
Capacity limits are often not a vague “we need AI” problem. They show up as one repeatable workflow decision: do you keep answering the same customer questions by hand, or do you build a bounded system for the routine part and keep judgment with you? For a small business owner, that is usually the real comparison: another hire, more manual work, or a narrow automation investment.

The useful diagnostic is simple. Ask whether the requests come from a small set of common patterns, or whether each case is genuinely different. If the work is mostly repeatable, AI can help with the standard part. If each case needs live judgment, context, or a human call, forcing automation is the wrong move. That is not a failure; it is a boundary.

That is the kind of question we use in Bareni’s diagnostic. We look at one recurring workflow, say honestly whether AI fits, and if it does, define pilot scope, fixed price, and measures. That describes intended pilot scope, not an observed customer result. Human approval stays in place for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

The point is usually less dramatic than people expect. Capacity limits often hide in one boring process that keeps landing on the desk. Start there, and keep the rest human.
